blocks.passage:
Negotiating across borders is rarely about the price alone. It is about understanding how the other side makes decisions — who is really in the room, who will say yes later, how much face and hierarchy matter, and how silence is interpreted.

In some cultures, silence means the other side is thinking and you should wait. In others, it means discomfort and you should fill it. In some cultures, a quick agreement is a sign of trust; in others, it is a sign of carelessness. These differences are rarely taught — they are learned by paying attention.

The safe defaults are: slow down, ask more questions than you answer, use hedging language to avoid sounding final, and confirm everything in writing in the other side's time zone.

items.why: "Negotiating across borders is rarely about the price alone."

items.why: "who is really in the room, who will say yes later, how much face and hierarchy matter."

items.why: "In some cultures, silence means the other side is thinking… In others, it means discomfort."

audio.text:
This week you've got two negotiations back to back — a Japanese buyer on Tuesday, a Brazilian supplier on Thursday — and they could not be more different. Same skills, opposite defaults.

With the Japanese buyer, expect silence, and don't rush to fill it. A pause usually means they're thinking or consulting, not that something's wrong. The person doing the talking may not be the decision-maker — the real yes might come later, after an internal discussion. So don't push for a signature in the room. Plant the proposal, and let it travel up the hierarchy.

With the Brazilian supplier, it's warmer and faster. Silence there can feel awkward, so conversation flows. Relationships come first — spend time on the personal side before the numbers. But 'yes, of course' in the moment may be enthusiasm, not a firm commitment, so confirm the details afterwards.

The common thread for both: slow down, ask more than you tell, use hedging language so you don't sound final too early, and put everything in writing afterwards — in their time zone, not yours. Same toolkit, read the room differently.

the person who does the talking
